level1.text: A square wire loop of side $0.12\,\text{m}$ is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic flux density of the field is $0.35\,\text{T}$. How large is the magnetic flux through the loop? Give the answer in milliwebers.

A coil has $400$ turns. When a magnet is pushed into the coil, the magnetic flux through one turn grows steadily by $1.5\,\text{mWb}$ in $0.20\,\text{s}$. How large is the induced voltage in the coil?

A metal rod of length $0.25\,\text{m}$ moves at a speed of $2.0\,\text{m/s}$ in a uniform magnetic field of $0.40\,\text{T}$. The rod, its velocity and the field are mutually perpendicular. How large is the induced voltage between the ends of the rod?

A coil has $150$ turns. When a magnet is pulled away from the coil, an average induced voltage of $0.45\,\text{V}$ appears between the ends of the coil for $0.12\,\text{s}$. By how much did the magnetic flux through one turn change? Give the answer in milliwebers.

An induced voltage of $12\,\text{mV}$ is measured between the ends of a metal rod sliding on two rails. The distance between the rails is $0.30\,\text{m}$, and the magnetic flux density of the field perpendicular to the plane of the rails is $0.080\,\text{T}$. The rod moves perpendicular to itself. How large is the speed of the rod?

A strong bar magnet is at rest inside a coil, and a sensitive voltmeter is connected to the coil. The meter reads zero. Why is no induced voltage produced between the ends of the coil, even though a large magnetic flux passes through the coil?
level1.answer: The flux does not change, and the voltage depends only on the rate of change of the flux.

choices.text: The flux is so large that the wire of the coil cannot conduct a voltage.
choices.feedback: The size of the flux does not prevent a voltage from appearing. The voltage depends on the rate of change of the flux, not on the value of the flux; even a large flux gives zero voltage if it does not change.

choices.text: No current flows in the coil, and a voltage needs a current in order to appear.
choices.feedback: Cause and effect are the other way round: the voltage arises from the change in flux, and in a closed circuit it produces the current. There is no current because no voltage appears.

choices.text: The flux does not change, and the voltage depends only on the rate of change of the flux.
choices.feedback: Correct: according to the law of induction, the voltage is proportional to the rate of change of the flux $\Delta\Phi : \Delta t$. The flux of a magnet at rest is constant, so $\Delta\Phi = 0$ and the voltage is zero despite the large flux.

choices.text: The field and the coil are in the same place, so the field has no effect on the coil.
choices.feedback: The field affects the coil when the flux through it changes, for example when the magnet is moved. The flux of a stationary magnet is constant, and that alone is the reason the voltage is zero.

level1.text:
A coil has $120$ turns, and when a magnet is pushed into the coil, an induced voltage of $0.90\,\text{V}$ appears between its ends.

A second coil is otherwise similar (the same area), but it has $300$ turns. The magnet is pushed into it in the same way and at the same speed. How large is the induced voltage between the ends of the second coil?

A metal rod of length $0.50\,\text{m}$ moves at a speed of $0.60\,\text{m/s}$ in a uniform magnetic field. The rod, its velocity and the field are mutually perpendicular, and an induced voltage of $18\,\text{mV}$ is measured between the ends of the rod. How large is the magnetic flux density of the field?

Consider five situations in which an induced voltage can arise. The values are example values, and the flux of one turn means the magnetic flux through one turn of the coil.

Situation A: the flux of one turn of a coil of $200$ turns grows steadily by $3.0\,\text{mWb}$ in $0.50\,\text{s}$.

Situation B: the flux of one turn of a coil of $50$ turns grows steadily by $6.0\,\text{mWb}$ in $0.10\,\text{s}$.

Situation C: around the iron core of a large electromagnet there is a coil of $500$ turns. The current of the electromagnet is constant, and a flux of $8.0\,\text{mWb}$ passes through one turn.

Situation D: a metal rod of length $0.50\,\text{m}$ moves at a speed of $4.0\,\text{m/s}$ in a homogeneous magnetic field of $0.30\,\text{T}$. The rod, its velocity and the field are perpendicular to each other.

Situation E: the flux through a single wire loop decreases steadily by $40\,\text{mWb}$ in $0.020\,\text{s}$.

Calculate the magnitude $|e|$ of the induced voltage in each situation and put the situations in order.
level1.prompt: Put the situations in order of the magnitude $|e|$ of the induced voltage, from smallest to largest.
level1.answer: Situation C ($0\,\text{V}$), situation D ($0.60\,\text{V}$), situation A ($1.2\,\text{V}$), situation E ($2.0\,\text{V}$), situation B ($3.0\,\text{V}$).

level2.text: A flexible wire loop is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of $0.80\,\text{T}$. The loop is squeezed so that its area decreases steadily from $200\,\text{cm}^2$ to $50\,\text{cm}^2$ in $0.25\,\text{s}$. How large is the induced voltage in the loop? Give the answer in millivolts.

A coil has $50$ turns. The graph shows the magnetic flux $\Phi$ through one turn as a function of time $t$. What is the greatest absolute value of the induced voltage of the coil in the interval $0$–$0.70\,\text{s}$? Read the necessary values from the graph.

Two horizontal metal rails are $0.40\,\text{m}$ apart, and their ends are joined by a $2.0\,\Omega$ resistor. A transverse metal rod slides on the rails at a speed of $3.0\,\text{m/s}$. The magnetic flux density of the vertical magnetic field is $0.50\,\text{T}$. The resistance of the rails and the rod is very small. How large is the current through the resistor?

A square coil of side $5.0\,\text{cm}$ with $20$ turns is pulled at a steady speed of $0.25\,\text{m/s}$ into a region of uniform magnetic field. The field of $0.30\,\text{T}$ is perpendicular to the plane of the coil, and the leading side of the coil is parallel to the edge of the field.

How large is the induced voltage in the coil during the time in which the coil is entering the field? Give the answer in millivolts.

A coil has $120$ turns. The table shows sample data: the magnetic flux $\Phi$ through one turn at different moments while the coil is moved in a magnetic field. The flux changes roughly steadily during each $0.10\,\text{s}$ interval.

What is the greatest absolute value of the induced voltage of the coil during the measurement period?

level2.text:
Students investigate how the induced voltage depends on the speed of the motion. A metal rod is moved at a steady speed $v$ on horizontal rails in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of the rails, and the voltage $e$ between the ends of the rod is measured.

The rod and the field are perpendicular, and the distance between the rails, that is, the length of the rod in the field, is $0.20\,\text{m}$. The table shows sample data.

Plot the measurement points in a $(v, e)$ coordinate system and fit a straight line through the origin to the points. How large is the magnetic flux density of the field? Use the slope of the line.

A student solves a problem: “A metal rod of length $0.30\,\text{m}$ moves at a speed of $2.0\,\text{m/s}$ in a uniform magnetic field of $0.50\,\text{T}$. The rod is perpendicular to the field but moves in the direction of the field.”

The student calculates $e = vBl = 2.0\,\text{m/s} \cdot 0.50\,\text{T} \cdot 0.30\,\text{m} = 0.30\,\text{V}$ and states that a voltage of $0.30\,\text{V}$ appears between the ends of the rod.

What is wrong in the calculation?
level2.answer: The velocity is in the direction of the field, so the magnetic force on the electrons is zero.

choices.text: The voltage is determined by the mass and the speed of the rod, so the magnetic flux density should not be used.
choices.feedback: The mass of the rod does not affect the induced voltage. The voltage appears when the field exerts a force on the electrons of the rod, and its size depends on the speed, the magnetic flux density and the length.

choices.text: A voltage appears only in a closed circuit, so there is no voltage between the ends of the rod.
choices.feedback: A voltage $e = vBl$ appears between the ends of a moving rod even when the rod is not part of a closed circuit. In a closed circuit the voltage also produces a current.

choices.text: The voltage of a rod moving at a steady speed is always zero, because the motion is not accelerating.
choices.feedback: The voltage does not require accelerating motion. For example, the voltage of a rod moving at a steady speed perpendicular to the field is constant, $vBl$.

choices.text: The velocity is in the direction of the field, so the magnetic force on the electrons is zero.
choices.feedback: Correct: the formula $e = vBl$ holds when the velocity, the rod and the field are mutually perpendicular. No magnetic force acts on an electron moving in the direction of the field, no charge collects at the ends of the rod, and the voltage is zero.

level2.text: A coil has $200$ turns. The graph shows the magnetic flux $\Phi$ through one turn as a function of time $t$. The direction of the flux through the turn reverses during the measurement, so the flux also takes negative values. What is the magnitude of the average induced voltage of the coil in the interval $0$–$0.40\,\text{s}$? Read the values you need from the graph.

level3.text: A train travels at a speed of $200\,\text{km/h}$ on a horizontal track. The track gauge of the Finnish railways is $1524\,\text{mm}$ (Finnish Transport Infrastructure Agency), and the metal axle of a pair of wheels extends from rail to rail. The vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field in southern Finland is about $50\,\mu\text{T}$ (WMM2025 model, NOAA/BGS). How large is the induced voltage between the ends of the axle at the rails? Give the answer in millivolts.

The Earth's magnetic field is measured with a flip coil. The coil has $100$ turns and an area of $0.020\,\text{m}^2$.

The coil is at first in a position in which its plane is perpendicular to the Earth's magnetic field. The coil is turned through half a turn in $0.10\,\text{s}$, and an average induced voltage of $2.0\,\text{mV}$ appears in the coil during this time.

How large is the magnetic flux density of the Earth's magnetic field? Give the answer in microteslas.

A bar magnet is dropped through a vertical coil of $300$ turns, and the voltage of the coil is measured with a data logger.

When the magnet enters the coil, the measurement shows a voltage pulse that is roughly triangular: the voltage rises from zero to a peak value of $0.90\,\text{V}$ and falls back to zero, and the pulse lasts $40\,\text{ms}$ in all. Before the drop the magnet is far from the coil.

How large is the magnetic flux through one turn on average when the pulse has ended and the magnet is in the middle of the coil? Give the answer in milliwebers.

A light cart with a transverse metal rod on top starts from rest and accelerates steadily on horizontal rails.

The distance between the rails, that is, the length of the rod in the field, is $0.40\,\text{m}$, and the magnetic flux density of the uniform field perpendicular to the plane of the rails is $0.25\,\text{T}$. The voltage $e$ between the ends of the rod is measured at moments $t$, where $t = 0$ is the moment of starting. The table shows sample data.

a) Using the formula $e = vBl$, explain why the voltage should grow in direct proportion to time, and determine the acceleration of the cart from the data.

b) Calculate the distance the cart travels during the first $1.2\,\text{s}$.

Write the justifications and calculations in your answer. The answer box takes the acceleration of part a).

data.caption: Sample data: voltage of the rod as a function of time

level3.text:
A bar magnet is dropped through a vertical coil of $250$ turns, and the voltage $e$ of the coil is recorded with an oscilloscope. Before the drop and after it the magnet is far from the coil.

The table shows sample data from the recording. The voltage is first positive, and when the magnet is in the middle of the coil, the voltage is roughly zero.

a) Estimate the area between the voltage graph and the time axis, that is, the sum of the products of voltage and time, during the first pulse, $t = 0$–$24\,\text{ms}$, and use it to calculate the greatest magnetic flux $\Phi$ through one turn.

b) Calculate the same quantity using the second pulse, $t = 24$–$48\,\text{ms}$, and explain why the pulses have opposite signs and why the second pulse is taller and narrower but has the same area.

Write the justifications and calculations in your answer. The answer box takes the magnetic flux of part a) in milliwebers.
